current_answer: 404 and 410 are heuristically cacheable, but HTTP does not require a cache to store them, set a universal heuristic lifetime, or reuse them outside the eligible GET/HEAD rules. If a cache stores a 404 for a versioned asset, restored bytes at the same URI may remain hidden while that response is fresh; this is an inference from HTTP reuse rules, not an observed deployment result. A new no-store response does not purge an older negative response, and Age alone does not identify a serving cache. See the 13 Oct 2026 missing-asset guide and dated report. Treat stale serving as a four-gate decision: the response must be storable at the named cache, its effective freshness lifetime must have elapsed, a bounded stale permission must apply, and no stronger revalidation rule may block stale reuse. Private caches normally use max-age; shared caches use s-maxage before max-age and Expires. stale-while-revalidate may return old bytes while a supporting cache validates, and stale-if-error may return them for a defined error, but neither extension grants storage, fixes a cache key, clears a browser or service worker, or guarantees implementation support. Under the portable RFC 9111 reading, do not treat either extension as an override for no-cache, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, or shared s-maxage revalidation semantics. Use ETag or Last-Modified for the ordinary validation path; If-None-Match wins when both conditions are present. Diagnose old content with named Cache-Status, Age, Via, provider fields, validators, and a correlated origin marker, while treating missing or single-hop evidence as unknown. This 25 Sep 2026 follow-up is documentation-only: no live stale response, 304, provider, browser, origin, purge, or invalidation result is claimed. A service-worker update also does not replace an open document or automatically clear script-managed Cache Storage: a candidate must be checked, installed, and activated; it normally waits for old clients, while skipWaiting can change their controller without reloading page code. Keep old fingerprinted assets and worker-cache entries through the supported compatibility window, then retire them under an explicit app policy. This 28 Sep 2026 follow-up is documentation-only; no browser, worker, origin, or deployment behavior was tested. For redirects, inspect the response to each requested URI: each hop has its own status, Location, key, and freshness. A stored redirect may retain an old Location; a current first hop does not prove later hops are current. Use explicit freshness or validation when a bounded route-change window matters. A new no-store response does not erase an older redirect. The final URL alone does not identify the hop or cache that supplied it. Browser HTTP-cache partitioning adds a user-agent context dimension: the Fetch Standard uses a network partition key with top-level site as its first component and leaves a second component null or implementation-defined. It does not replace RFC 9111 method/target-URI matching, Vary, storage, freshness, or validation, and it does not configure a CDN or proxy. Use private/no-store response policy for the intended storage audience; partitioning is not a privacy guarantee. Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit describe implementation-specific details and exceptions. The A/B context examples in the 4 Oct 2026 follow-up are expected, not tested; no browser or cache was measured. Request-side Cache-Control is a separate direction: RFC 9111 §5.2.1 treats request directives as advisory (caches MAY honor them), while response directives have a mandatory role. Request no-cache prefers validation but is not a universal origin-fetch command; no-store governs this exchange, not deletion of older entries; max-age, min-fresh, and max-stale express response-selection preferences; only-if-cached asks for stored content but is not a universal no-forwarding guarantee. None is a universal bypass or purge command, or proof of which cache honored it. The 7 Oct 2026 update is standards/documentation-only: no authorized runtime or browser/provider experiment was available, so examples are expected semantics, not live observations. POST response caching is a separate method-specific rule: RFC 9110 §9.3.3 requires explicit response freshness plus a Content-Location equal to the POST target URI; if stored and otherwise reusable, it may serve a later GET or HEAD, not POST. RFC 9111 separately requires unsafe-request write-through and, after a 2xx/3xx response, target-URI invalidation at caches traversed by that request only. These are protocol permissions/requirements, not evidence that a named cache stored or reused the response. The 10 Oct 2026 matrix is synthetic and expected only; no live test or implementation behavior is claimed. For the RFC 9111 Age calculation, a receiving cache derives current_age from corrected initial age plus resident time, using Date, Age, request/response timing, and the evaluation time. When a cache reuses a stored response without validation, it must generate Age equal to that response’s current_age at that response point. Age alone does not identify a cache or hop. The 16 Oct 2026 worked example is synthetic; no live endpoint, cache, browser, provider, or response header was tested. See the Age/current_age guide and dated report at /p/http-cache-field-guide/age-current-age and /p/http-cache-field-guide/reports/age-current-age-2026-10-16.html. For responses to requests carrying Authorization, RFC 9111 §3.5 lists must-revalidate, public, and s-maxage as permissions for shared-cache reuse; proxy-revalidate alone is not one of them and instead requires validation before stale reuse. Erratum 9004 proposed a no-behavior-change clarification, but the accessible archive record was Reported and its final disposition was not confirmed. This review did not test cache behavior; see the 19 Oct 2026 report at /p/http-cache-field-guide/reports/authorization-proxy-revalidate-2026-10-19.html. For a 304 validation, RFC 9111 §4.3.4 starts with responses that could otherwise have served the same target URI, reusable method, and request variant; the final freshness/stale gate is omitted, so stale entries can be candidates. A strong validator selects every matching candidate, but a nonmatching strong validator cannot fall through to weak matching. With no strong validator, a matching weak validator selects only the most recent candidate by Date. With no validator at all, only a single candidate that also has no validator qualifies. A 304 updates selected metadata, not representation bytes; the body comes from storage. The four-entry example is synthetic and no cache behavior was tested. See the 304 response selection guide and dated report. RFC 9213 standardizes CDN-Cache-Control as a targeted response policy, distinct from ordinary Cache-Control s-maxage, which applies to shared caches generally. A targeted cache selects the first valid, non-empty field on its ordered target list and uses those directives instead of ordinary Cache-Control and Expires; if none is usable, it falls back to ordinary HTTP rules. Freshness remains end-to-end: a CDN can consider a response fresh under a longer targeted lifetime while a downstream cache considers the same Age stale. Cloudflare documents its proprietary Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control ahead of CDN-Cache-Control, with product-specific forwarding, overrides, and Authorization interactions. These are standards and vendor-documentation findings only: no cache, browser, endpoint, zone, or deployment was tested. See the CDN-targeted Cache-Control guide and dated report. For versioned static resources, RFC 8246 defines response Cache-Control: immutable as a freshness-bounded assertion: while a stored response is fresh, clients SHOULD NOT conditionally revalidate it by default, including on reload, unless the user explicitly overrides that behavior. Once stale, ordinary revalidation rules apply. In the example Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable, max-age supplies the one-year lifetime; immutable does not set freshness, grant storage/public permission, change the key, or purge an old URL. RFC 9111 gives s-maxage precedence for shared-cache freshness if it is present. Current MDN documentation notes a Chrome-specific reload/subresource implementation caveat; this does not establish behavior across browsers or versions. The 28 Oct 2026 review is standards/documentation-only: no browser, cache, endpoint, provider, response header, or versioned deployment was tested. See the immutable response guide and dated report.

catalogue_card.question: How can web developers choose correct HTTP cache headers and diagnose stale content without accidentally caching private responses?
catalogue_card.text: When old bytes appear, separate storage permission, browser/private max-age, shared s-maxage, bounded stale permission, and conditional validation. Use named-hop evidence to distinguish an expected stale/revalidation path from an unexplained copy, and keep private/sensitive responses out of shared storage. For service-worker deploys, distinguish worker activation from page reload and application-directed Cache Storage cleanup. For a moved URL that still lands at an old destination, record each redirect response and Location separately; do not infer the supplying cache from the final URL or Age alone. Browser partitioning can add a top-level-site dimension to browser-local HTTP-cache selection, but it does not replace HTTP policy or configure a shared intermediary; the cited context comparison is expected, not tested. A request Cache-Control field is an advisory preference, not response policy or a universal bypass/origin-contact/purge command; see the 7 Oct 2026 request-directive guide for the six directive roles and limits. For POST responses, explicit freshness plus same-target Content-Location makes later GET/HEAD reuse eligible, not guaranteed; unsafe POST forwarding and 2xx/3xx invalidation at traversed caches are separate, non-global rules. See the 10 Oct 2026 guide; its cases are expected only, not live-tested. A 404/410 is heuristically cacheable but not necessarily stored, and status does not give a universal lifetime. A new no-store response does not clear an older negative entry; Age alone does not identify a hop. See the 13 Oct missing-asset guide. RFC 9111 calculates current_age from corrected initial age plus resident time; Age is an input, not a timeless value, and a cache reusing an unvalidated stored response must emit Age equal to its calculated current_age at that response point. See the Age/current_age guide and synthetic worked report. For an Authorization request, RFC 9111 §3.5 lists must-revalidate, public, and s-maxage as shared-cache reuse permissions; proxy-revalidate alone is not permission and instead governs validation after staleness. Erratum 9004 proposed a no-behavior-change clarification, but its final disposition was not confirmed from the accessible archive record. See the 19 Oct 2026 report at /p/http-cache-field-guide/reports/authorization-proxy-revalidate-2026-10-19.html; no cache implementation behavior was tested. For a 304, the request-compatible candidate set is followed by strong-validator matches, otherwise the most recent weak match, or a singleton validator-less exception; the 304 supplies metadata, not a replacement body. See the 22 Oct 2026 304 response selection guide and synthetic report; no implementation was tested. For CDN policy, RFC 9213 uses an ordered target list: the first valid non-empty targeted field replaces ordinary Cache-Control and Expires for that cache, while s-maxage remains a shared-cache directive generally. The CDN-targeted Cache-Control guide explains Cloudflare-specific field precedence and forwarding separately. The synthetic example and vendor documentation are not live cache or zone evidence. For versioned static resources, RFC 8246’s response `immutable` recommendation is limited to freshness: it discourages conditional validation while the stored response is fresh, allows explicit user override, and stops governing revalidation when stale. `max-age` supplies the example lifetime; `immutable` does not grant shared storage or purge the old URL. The MDN Chrome caveat is specific to subresources on reload. No browser or cache was tested in the 28 Oct 2026 review.

summary: The checks common to CloudFront and Cloudflare are representation review, storage audience, explicit browser/shared freshness, validators, key review, named-hop evidence, and downstream limits.
Use no-store when intentional HTTP-cache retention is unacceptable; use private, no-cache when browser retention with validation is acceptable and shared storage is not allowed.
For safely public mutable content, set max-age and s-maxage deliberately and use validators; s-maxage controls shared-cache freshness separately from browser max-age.
For immutable changed bytes, prefer a new versioned or content-hash URL; a new URL is not deletion of the old URL.
If-None-Match is evaluated before If-Modified-Since when both conditions are present; a 304 does not identify the serving hop.
The minimum HTTP cache-key model is method plus target URI, with Vary and deployment-specific key inputs layered on top; TTL cannot repair a key collision.
In an incident, first ask whether a network request occurred, then inspect named-hop fields and correlate a redacted origin marker with a counter.
Age, Cache-Status, Via, CF-Cache-Status, and CloudFront Server-Timing metrics are scoped evidence with different standards or vendor boundaries; missing fields are unknown.
CloudFront positive minimum TTL and response-header policies are CloudFront-specific; a viewer Cache-Control value is not proof of edge TTL.
Cloudflare Origin Cache Control, matching Cache Rule, Edge/Browser TTL, custom key, and purge scope are separate Cloudflare controls; keep them separate from CloudFront and HTTP rules.
A named-provider purge or invalidation is not universal eviction: browser, service-worker, corporate-proxy, history, other edge, and application copies remain downstream limits.
This run is documentation-only/no live provider capture; no deployment, incident, privacy, freshness, purge, invalidation, or browser result is claimed.
A stale response needs four gates: allowed storage, an elapsed effective lifetime, an applicable stale permission, and no stronger prohibition blocking reuse.
Private caches normally apply max-age; shared caches apply s-maxage before max-age and Expires. The same object can be fresh in one cache and stale in another.
stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error are bounded, support-dependent permissions; they do not grant storage, shared safety, key correctness, purge, or browser/service-worker eviction.
Under the portable RFC 9111 reading, do not treat stale extensions as overrides for no-cache, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, or shared s-maxage revalidation semantics.
A 304 permits reuse of stored bytes at the evaluating recipient; it does not identify the hop, prove origin contact, or prove application freshness.
Cache-Status fwd=stale, fwd-status, hit, ttl, Age, Via, provider fields, and origin markers are scoped evidence. Missing fields are unknown.
Use a versioned URL for changed public assets; versioning and a named-provider purge have different scopes and neither clears every downstream copy.

A worker update does not replace an open document or automatically clear Cache Storage. A successful candidate normally waits for old registration clients; skipWaiting may change their controller without reloading their in-memory code. Keep old fingerprinted assets and caches until an explicit compatibility policy permits retirement.

clients.claim() is separate from skipWaiting(): an active worker may take control of eligible matching clients outside its current controlled set. Neither operation reloads a page or proves application compatibility.

For an old-asset incident, record page and worker build markers, registration states and URLs, current page controller, exact requested asset, worker cache decision, and named downstream evidence. No service-worker behavior was measured in the 28 Sep 2026 documentation-only run.
A redirect response belongs to the URI requested at that hop; every redirect in a chain is a separate cache candidate with its own Location and freshness.
301 and 308 are heuristically cacheable under RFC 9110; 302, 303, and 307 are not heuristic by default, though explicit cacheability can permit storage. No status guarantees actual reuse.
Use explicit max-age/Expires or validation when route changes need a bounded stale-target window; no-store on a new response does not delete an older redirect.
Capture status, Location, request method, cache metadata, and named-hop evidence for every response. A final URL, Age, or missing header alone does not identify the cache layer.

The Fetch Standard models user-agent HTTP-cache partitioning with top-level site as a key component; RFC 9111 matching, Vary, storage, freshness, and validation still apply, and an intermediary has its own key and policy.

Browser partitioning is not a substitute for private/no-store policy or a privacy guarantee. Chrome, Firefox, and WebKit details differ; cross-context examples in the 4 Oct 2026 documentation-only report are expected, not measured.
RFC 9111 request Cache-Control directives are advisory: caches MAY honor them, but request fields do not rewrite response policy or target one named cache.

Request no-cache prefers validation; request no-store governs storage of that exchange, not deletion of older entries; request max-age/min-fresh/max-stale express response-selection preferences; only-if-cached asks for stored content but does not guarantee every cache will avoid forwarding.
Request directives are not universal bypass, origin-contact, purge, or privacy commands. A 304, missing Age, or absent Cache-Status does not identify every hop.
The 7 Oct 2026 request-directive examples are synthetic RFC-based expectations. No authorized runtime or browser/provider experiment was available and no live cache behavior is claimed.

A POST response meets the POST-specific eligibility condition only with explicit freshness and a Content-Location equal to the request target URI; a stored response may later serve GET or HEAD, not POST.
A cache may decline to store or reuse a POST response even when those conditions are met; general storage, target/method match, freshness, no-store, and other requirements still apply.

Unsafe requests are written through before a cache responds. After a 2xx/3xx response, a traversed cache must invalidate stored response(s) for the target URI; this does not reach caches outside the request path or prove retention of the newly received POST response.
The 10 Oct 2026 POST examples and matrix are synthetic RFC-based expectations. No authorized endpoint, cache, browser, provider, or implementation was tested.
RFC 9110 makes 404 and 410 heuristically cacheable; that permits reuse but does not require storage or provide a universal negative-response lifetime.
If a cache stores a 404 for a versioned URI, restored bytes at that same URI may remain hidden while the negative response is fresh; this is a standards inference, not an observed deployment result.
A new response with no-store does not purge an older stored 404. no-cache may permit storage but requires validation before reuse.
Age reports estimated response age and, by itself, does not identify the cache or hop that supplied a response.
The 13 Oct 2026 negative-caching review is standards/documentation-only; no endpoint, cache, provider, browser, or deployment was tested.

RFC 9111 §4.2.3 calculates a stored response’s current_age from corrected_initial_age plus resident_time, using Date, Age, request/response timing, and the evaluation time; Age alone is not a timeless reading.

For an unvalidated stored-response reuse, RFC 9111 §4 requires the cache to generate Age equal to the stored response’s current_age at that response point; Age alone does not identify a specific cache or hop.
The 16 Oct 2026 Age/current_age arithmetic is fully synthetic. No live endpoint, browser, cache, provider, or response header was tested.
For a request carrying Authorization, RFC 9111 §3.5 lists must-revalidate, public, and s-maxage as response directives that can permit shared-cache reuse; proxy-revalidate is not on that list.
RFC 9111 §5.2.2.8 uses proxy-revalidate to require validation before a shared cache reuses a stale response; it does not itself grant Authorization-request reuse.

Erratum 9004 proposed a no-behavior-change clarification. The accessible archive record was Reported and a co-author reply said REJECT, but the final formal disposition was not confirmed. No cache implementation behavior was tested.

After a 304, RFC 9111 §4.3.4 uses request-compatible candidates and a first-match strong, weak, or narrow no-validator branch; the 22 Oct example is synthetic, and 304 updates metadata rather than carrying replacement bytes.

RFC 9213 defines CDN-Cache-Control as a targeted field; a cache selects its first valid, non-empty listed field instead of merging it with ordinary Cache-Control or Expires, and falls back to ordinary rules when no listed field is usable.
s-maxage is an ordinary Cache-Control directive for shared caches generally, not a CDN-only control.

Cloudflare documents Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control ahead of CDN-Cache-Control and describes product-specific forwarding, overrides, and Authorization interactions; these rules do not establish the behavior of any live zone or another provider.
Targeted lifetimes do not reset end-to-end Age or fix cache-key/privacy mismatches. The freshness matrix is synthetic; no browser, endpoint, cache, or Cloudflare zone was tested.

For a versioned static resource, `immutable` discourages conditional validation only while the stored response is fresh; `max-age` supplies the example lifetime, and a force reload can explicitly override the optimization.
uncertainty: No authorized CloudFront distribution, Cloudflare zone, endpoint, controlled origin, vendor log, browser or HTTP-client capture, purge/invalidation operation, or analytics was supplied.
Actual matching rules, cache keys, POP/tier state, object residency, response rewriting, current age, and downstream copies require a live topology.
A fresh browser, direct client, one POP, one provider status, or one marker test cannot establish absence of copies or leakage everywhere.
No request may reflect history/back-forward cache or a service worker; browser DevTools controls change the experiment and do not bypass every downstream layer.
A response header, 200, 304, missing Age, missing Cache-Status, browser label, purge receipt, or invalidation completion cannot identify every producer or prove global eviction.
Cloudflare documentation describes no-cache differently in generic and OCC-specific contexts; the actual zone state and an authorized synthetic capture are needed to resolve it.
Provider-specific TTL, key, status, and purge behavior can vary by product, plan, configuration, tier, POP, and time; do not generalize either named provider.

The next useful live probe needs a fixed authorized URL, sanitized origin marker/counter, selected provider configuration, controlled request variants, named vantage, and permission to capture and if necessary purge synthetic objects.
The RFCs do not establish that a particular browser, CDN, reverse proxy, corporate proxy, service worker, or application cache implements stale extensions or applies the same precedence.

The shared s-maxage plus stale-* combination remains an implementation/configuration boundary when the strict RFC 9111 revalidation rule applies; any different named-provider result needs documentation and an authorized capture.

No browser session, authorized URL, response header capture, Age, Cache-Status, Via, provider field, 304, origin marker/counter, purge, invalidation, or analytics result was produced in this follow-up; all timing rows are expected and unexecuted.

No application, service-worker registration, browser/version, page/worker build marker, client inventory, Cache Storage contents, exact asset request, origin log, or permitted synthetic lifecycle test was supplied for the 28 Sep 2026 follow-up.

Actual update-check timing, install outcome, waiting-client population, controller changes, app compatibility, cache routing, asset retention, storage state, and safe retirement duration remain unknown without an authorized target-app test.

For the 1 Oct 2026 redirect follow-up, no endpoint, route migration, browser, cache, provider, origin, or analytics result was available or used; all scenarios are expected and unexecuted, and actual stored redirects, heuristic lifetimes, cache supplier, and user impact are unknown.

For the 4 Oct 2026 browser-partitioning follow-up, no browser/profile, HTTP request or response, endpoint, intermediary, CDN, cache, or cross-context result was tested; current key details, flags, selective resource exceptions, and named shared-cache behavior remain implementation-specific or unknown.

For the 7 Oct 2026 request-directive review, no authorized endpoint, cache chain, browser, provider configuration, request/response trace, origin counter, or analytics was available; whether any named implementation honors these advisory request preferences, forwards them, or resolves conflicting combinations remains unknown.

For the 10 Oct 2026 POST-response review, no authorized endpoint, topology, cache, browser, per-hop capture, or analytics was supplied; actual storage, reuse, forwarding, invalidation, and downstream copies remain untested and implementation-specific.

For the 13 Oct 2026 negative-caching follow-up, no endpoint, browser, provider, cache instance, origin log, request trace, purge, or analytics was available; actual storage, heuristic lifetime, cache key, response provenance, and post-restoration behavior remain unknown.

For the 16 Oct 2026 Age/current_age follow-up, no endpoint, response header, cache, browser, provider, or trace was available; the example does not establish an implementation’s emitted Age, path, clock synchronization, current age, or freshness behavior.
RFC 9213 does not establish that a named cache implements targeted fields or reveal its target list; support and configuration require product-specific evidence.
Cloudflare documentation does not establish a particular zone’s matching Cache Rules, Cache Response Rules, OCC state, Edge/Browser TTL, key, POP/tier path, headers, or resulting Age.
Malformed/empty header handling in a named configuration, date or Age rewriting, and a concrete downstream topology were not tested; all comparison values are synthetic.

For the 28 Oct 2026 `immutable` review, no browser, cache, endpoint, response header, provider, or versioned-asset deployment was tested; browser support and current-version behavior remain unverified.

This was a standards/documentation review only; no browser, cache, endpoint, provider, or response header was tested.
